candidateRows: Four exhaustive explanatory categories frame the case: later myth, sincere mistake, deliberate deception, or an actual resurrection.
This framework establishes the competing explanations that organize McLatchie's entire cumulative argument and his later elimination of alternatives.
After identifying himself as an evidentialist, McLatchie introduces an explanatory framework intended to organize his historical case for the resurrection.
Paul's early resurrection tradition and agreement with Peter, James, and the Twelve place the resurrection claim with the original apostles.
Locating the claim with the earliest apostolic witnesses directly supports the historical-resurrection case by challenging a later-legend explanation.
McLatchie uses Paul's Corinthian material, its received tradition, and Paul's asserted consistency with other apostles to argue for an early apostolic origin.
Luke's access to Paul and Jerusalem leaders, together with features of the Acts travel narrative, supports Acts as an informed report of the apostles' resurrection proclamation.
The move supplies a transmission route from Jerusalem leadership to Acts, reinforcing the claim that resurrection preaching originated with the apostles.
McLatchie connects the Pentecost proclamation to Luke's claimed presence with Paul and Jerusalem leaders, then invokes narrative travel details to support that access.
Distinctive personal knowledge in the Fourth Gospel supports its derivation from the beloved disciple and therefore from an eyewitness source.
Eyewitness grounding for John would strengthen the historical status of a resurrection-appearance report and further oppose the later-myth account.
The argument links the named high-priestly servant and related courtyard knowledge to the beloved disciple, whom the Gospel presents as its witness-author.
The reported appearances were collective, multisensory, conversational, physical, and extended over time, making sincere perceptual error an inadequate explanation.
This move directly distinguishes the reported encounters from conditions associated with ordinary eyewitness error and targets the sincere-mistake alternative.
The skeptical position, attributed to Dillahunty's prior debate arguments, that eyewitness testimony is notoriously unreliable.
Having argued that the claim reaches the apostles, McLatchie addresses whether those apostles could nevertheless have been honestly mistaken about their experiences.
The apostles' willingness to suffer and die, along with the transformations of James and Peter, counts against deliberate fabrication and favors resurrection as the explanation.
The passage targets the conspiracy explanation by arguing that central claimants knowingly accepted grave costs and underwent otherwise unexplained transformations.
McLatchie invokes reported martyrdom traditions and changes in James and Peter to argue that the original claimants were not promoting something they knew was false.
Strong historical support should meet demanding standards analogous to legal proof, including physical corroboration and identifiable witnesses available for examination.
This move establishes Dillahunty's governing standard for evaluating the resurrection reports and the criteria by which he finds testimonial material insufficient.
McLatchie's opening claim that the presented apostolic and Gospel material provides a strong public historical case for resurrection.
Dillahunty begins his opening by characterizing the available material as hearsay and develops a courtroom analogy for what strong, testable support would require.
The biblical reports lack secure custody, sworn or examinable testimony, known provenance, and physical corroboration, so their resurrection claims cannot be adequately tested.
The move directly denies that the surviving Christian reports satisfy the motion's demand for strong historical support and challenges their reliability and testability.
McLatchie's reliance on Paul, Acts, and John as sufficiently reliable routes to original eyewitness resurrection testimony.
Applying his legal analogy, Dillahunty argues that anonymous, copied, potentially altered accounts cannot be cross-examined or independently checked against physical remains or records.
A God who wanted rational belief in the resurrection would provide and preserve far better evidence than the indirect, untestable reports available.
This directly argues that the surviving evidence is inconsistent with the quality and accessibility expected if a concerned God had performed the resurrection.
After an audio interruption, Matt resumes his opening case by contrasting the evidence a communicative God could supply with anonymous hearsay that cannot realistically be investigated.
The resurrection reports do not approach strong historical evidence because they lack investigable physical corroboration, identifiable witnesses, and reliable sourcing.
The passage applies the skeptical historical standard directly to the resurrection record and concludes that its documentary basis cannot establish the claimed event.
Matt emphasizes the exceptional importance of the claim, compares the available material with evidence needed to file and prove a case, and characterizes the writings as unsourced tradition.
Anecdotal testimony in untraceable ancient writings cannot become strong evidence merely by accumulation, especially when comparable testimony supports rejected supernatural claims.
This supplies the operative evidentiary standard behind the skeptical case and argues that accepting the Christian reports would also admit witchcraft and alien-abduction claims.
Using a hypothetical resurrection claim, Matt stresses the inability to inspect the allegedly raised person, then contrasts anonymous testimony with physical evidence and tested eyewitness accounts.
The proposed explanatory alternatives begin too far downstream by assuming the reported death and resurrection events, while overlooking legendary development of the story.
This challenges the framing of the pro case itself by denying that reported events must first be accepted and then explained through a restricted hypothesis set.
Jonathan's opening presented a limited set of hypotheses intended to explain the disciples' reported resurrection experiences.
At the end of his opening, Matt argues that the existence of a resurrection story does not establish the underlying events and says legendary formation remains an alternative.
Legend was included among the proposed alternatives, and early Pauline and Lukan material connects the resurrection proclamation to the original apostles and varied encounters.
This defends the completeness of the pro explanation set and the early apostolic provenance of the resurrection claim against the charge of later legendary development.
Matt argued that Jonathan's explanatory framework omitted legend and assumed the reported resurrection events rather than establishing them.
Jonathan restates four alternatives, identifies legend as the first, and appeals to First Corinthians and Luke-Acts to trace preaching and reported encounters back to apostolic sources.
Documentary evidence can be strong when multiple mutually corroborating sources converge, and that cumulative record supports both appearances and the empty tomb.
The passage directly defends the central pro contention that historical documents can collectively supply strong evidence with explanatory power and scope for resurrection.
Matt maintained that strong evidence would require physical and investigable support, while the available documentary testimony is inherently weak.
Jonathan rejects a physical-evidence-only standard, invokes analysis of statements from deceased witnesses, and presents appearances and the empty tomb as convergent observations.
The anonymity objection is not established because the lost originals may have carried names, while contextual and internal considerations support Luke and John as informed witnesses.
Authorship and eyewitness access bear directly on whether the documents underlying the resurrection case can be treated as informed and historically credible testimony.
Matt characterized the Gospel material as anonymous, unsourceable writings whose purported eyewitness origins cannot be investigated or confirmed.

Jonathan argues that absent original manuscripts prevent certainty about initial anonymity, says Luke's address to Theophilus suggests known authorship, and treats Johannine material as self-professed eyewitness testimony.
A miraculous claim properly receives a low prior probability, but sufficiently strong cumulative documentary evidence can overcome even an extremely small prior.
This addresses the core inference standard for an extraordinary event and explains how the pro side believes historical evidence can rationally support resurrection despite its low prior.
Matt argued that resurrection is an extraordinary supernatural claim for which ordinary anecdotal testimony cannot satisfy an appropriately demanding evidentiary standard.

Jonathan concedes greater skepticism toward miracles, distinguishes prior from posterior probability, illustrates cumulative confirmation with a lottery example, and suggests theism can also affect the prior.
Legend means the reported events themselves may be unwarranted, and sincere belief or martyrdom cannot validate them because equally sincere false beliefs are widespread.
This preserves the principal skeptical alternative to the resurrection inference and challenges sincerity-based support through parity with many acknowledged false belief systems.
Jonathan replied that legend was already one of his four alternatives and defended the early, sincere apostolic proclamation of resurrection.

Matt distinguishes his legend objection from simply overlooking a category, rejects assuming the narrative events, and argues that the proposed standard would validate many incompatible religions and conspiracies.

A supernatural resurrection is not a better explanation than ordinary human error when the underlying event is only asserted and the principal Pauline, Lukan, and Johannine sources are indirect or unverifiable.
The passage attacks both the explanatory inference to resurrection and the claimed quality of its main documentary foundations, reaching the debate's central historical question.
Jonathan argued that resurrection best explains the reported evidence and that Paul, Luke-Acts, and John provide corroborating, apostolically connected testimony.
Matt says a claim need not be explained as an event before it is established, then argues Paul was not an eyewitness, Luke's witnesses cannot be examined, and John's attribution remains unproved.
A defensible supernatural conclusion requires evidence establishing both supernatural reality and a causal connection to the material event.
This states the skeptical evidential threshold at the heart of the motion and answers the allegation that his inability to specify evidence exposes a defective epistemology.
McLatchie's earlier contention that Dillahunty cannot specify what evidence would persuade him and therefore applies a flawed epistemology.
Dillahunty argues that he need not predict the form of adequate evidence; the required demonstration concerns supernatural causation, and a capable God could provide substantially clearer evidence.
Anonymous, mutually inconsistent, and untestable reports do not establish an empty tomb, crucifixion details, or resurrection strongly enough to satisfy the motion.
The passage directly denies that the surviving sources amount to strong resurrection evidence and explains the principal defects alleged against those sources.
McLatchie's case that the empty tomb and resurrection reports require a better skeptical explanation and cumulatively constitute strong historical evidence.

Dillahunty says there is no independently established empty tomb to explain, emphasizes disagreement among resurrection narratives and lack of investigable access, and concludes that the available reports are insufficient.
Paul is not an eyewitness to the crucifixion merely because he relays what other apostles proclaimed, and the underlying alleged witnesses remain inaccessible.
This challenges a principal route from Pauline and apostolic material to firsthand testimony, limiting the reports to indirect and presently untestable transmission.
McLatchie's appeal to testimony in Paul, Acts, and the Gospels, including Paul's access to Peter and James, as evidence for Jesus's death.

Dillahunty distinguishes witnessing apostolic proclamation from witnessing the event itself, disputes treating Paul as a crucifixion witness, and stresses the absence of directly investigable reports from the named figures.
Assuming that Luke had access to a large body of Jerusalem witnesses presupposes the historical truth of the reported events and is therefore circular.
The objection attacks the inferential legitimacy of using presumed witness availability to authenticate Acts when the existence and status of those witnesses are disputed.
McLatchie's assertion that Luke traveled with Paul and consequently enjoyed ample access to a treasure trove of living witnesses in Jerusalem.
After McLatchie infers that Luke could consult many witnesses, Dillahunty argues that calling them witnesses already assumes the very historicity that the argument is meant to establish.
A testimony's claim is not itself its supporting evidence; credibility must come from independently assessable reliability that anonymous Gospel authors do not supply.
This supplies the central epistemic reason offered for rejecting the reports as strong evidence: their authorship, reliability, and factual basis cannot be adequately investigated.
McLatchie's argument that a trusted person's assertion is itself evidence and that Dillahunty's claim-versus-evidence distinction is epistemically mistaken.

Dillahunty says a trusted friend's track record, rather than the friend's bare assertion, supports belief; because the Gospel authors and their reliability cannot be examined, their testimony cannot reasonably establish resurrection.
Numerous historical confirmations and undesigned interconnections among the Gospels and Acts cumulatively support their substantial trustworthiness and informed proximity to events.
The argument provides the pro side's principal bridge from ordinary historical cross-confirmation to warranted reliance on the sources when evaluating less directly checkable resurrection material.
Dillahunty's contention that anonymous personal testimony lacks independently assessable reliability and cannot reasonably support a resurrection conclusion.
McLatchie presents an inductive cumulative case for source reliability and illustrates it through an interlocking chronology in John and Mark that he treats as an undesigned coincidence.
Shared or compatible mundane details may arise through common stories or literary dependence and do not validate extraordinary resurrection assertions.
This directly contests the proposed inference from interlocking ordinary details to resurrection reliability, thereby challenging a central evidential bridge in the pro case.
McLatchie's undesigned-coincidence example claiming that Mark and John's interlocking chronology supports substantial Gospel trustworthiness beyond directly checkable details.

Dillahunty argues that uncertain dating, circulating traditions, and possible literary dependence undercut independence; even genuine agreement on ordinary facts would not establish accuracy about resurrection or eliminate bias and honest error.
Interconnections spanning distinct Gospel traditions remain evidential even under an oral-source hypothesis, which is less simple than concluding that the narrated events occurred.
This preserves the pro reliability argument against the con side's main alternative explanation for apparent coincidences, namely derivation from circulating oral tradition.
Dillahunty's argument that apparent independence can result from multiple writers drawing different versions from a previously circulating oral tradition.

McLatchie responds that interlocks occur across distinct narrative units rather than a single comprehensive oral source, says prior oral derivation would not remove the coincidence, and favors real events as the simpler account.
Access to a shared story and apparent sincerity cannot establish eyewitness accuracy, especially when comparable supernatural testimony from other religions is rejected.
The passage attacks both testimonial reliability and selective treatment of miracle claims, pressing a parity challenge that bears directly on whether Christian reports count as strong evidence.
McLatchie's claim that cumulative interlocking details show the Gospel and Acts authors were close to the facts, reliably informed, and habitually truthful.

Dillahunty distinguishes common access from firsthand observation, notes that sincere eyewitnesses can be mistaken, compares trusted but unsupported religious testimony, and asks how Christian miracle reporters differ from analogous claimants elsewhere.

If the resurrection narratives derive from early apostolic eyewitness testimony, their reported encounter patterns require explanation, while source trustworthiness counts against deliberate fabrication.
This reconnects the disputed reliability discussion to the resurrection itself and identifies how eyewitness provenance and general trustworthiness constrain competing explanatory hypotheses.
Dillahunty's challenge that sincere or apparently reliable religious reporters may be mistaken and that Christian miracle testimony lacks an advantage over rival religions.

McLatchie argues that eyewitness-based Gospel and Acts traditions transmit early apostolic encounter claims that must be compared across explanatory hypotheses, with substantial trustworthiness providing evidence against intentional deception.
The substantial trustworthiness of the accounts and the apostles' willingness to die for their testimony count against deliberate fabrication.
It addresses deliberate deception, one of the principal alternative explanations that the historical resurrection case seeks to eliminate.
Dillahunty's challenge that Christian miracle reports lack a principled advantage over comparable religious testimony.
McLatchie moves from claimed eyewitness grounding to hypothesis comparison, arguing that general reliability and martyrdom support sincerity without conclusively proving it.
McLatchie offers no principled epistemic distinction between Christian testimony and rejected miracle reports from other religions, while relying only on indirect biblical claims.
It directly contests whether the surviving Christian reports meet a strong evidential standard and argues that the proposed method cannot discriminate true miracle claims from false ones.
McLatchie's appeal to trustworthy Gospel testimony and apostolic sincerity as evidence favoring the resurrection reports.

Dillahunty presses comparative religious cases, asks for nonbiblical support, distinguishes stories from physical corroboration, and argues that indistinguishability from false reports defeats the case.
Although weak and anecdotal material can count as evidence, the resurrection case presented does not amount to strong evidence because it rests on anonymous accounts in a favored book.
The move clarifies the governing evidential threshold and directly argues that the offered material fails the motion's requirement of strong evidence rather than denying all evidence categorically.
McLatchie's accusation that Dillahunty simply dismisses evidence and the surrounding confusion over whether the topic requires merely evidence or strong evidence.
During the transition to questions, Dillahunty distinguishes the existence of evidence from evidential sufficiency and characterizes the presented sources as too weak to justify belief.

The disputed and apparently supplemented ending of Mark undermines broad appeals to the Gospel's trustworthiness and illustrates the difficulty of identifying reliable portions without independent investigation.
It challenges the textual reliability of a principal resurrection source and thereby attacks the inference from vivid narrative details to accurate eyewitness memory.
The questioner's claim that Mark's historical present, vividness, and small details are best explained as reflections of eyewitness memory.

Dillahunty separates an author's apparent sincerity from factual accuracy, then uses the longer ending of Mark to argue that textual transmission complicates claims of comprehensive Gospel reliability.
Gospel trustworthiness is supported inductively, and extraordinary testimony should be assessed by comparing sincere error, deliberate deception, and the detailed circumstances of each case.
It states the methodological engine of the affirmative case: infer source reliability inductively and adjudicate extraordinary reports through case-specific comparison of competing explanations.
Dillahunty's contention that local textual accuracy does not establish global Gospel reliability and his hypothetical about trusting an otherwise reliable person's alien-abduction report.
McLatchie agrees that bare trust is insufficient, but argues that multiple witnesses and case particulars require analysis of whether testimony reflects deception, sincere mistake, or reality.
The resurrection case still lacks a non-question-begging basis for accepting its witnesses while rejecting religious and alien-abduction claimants who also present extraordinary testimony.
It targets the affirmative method's discriminatory power, arguing that asserted confidence in Christian witnesses does not itself supply a foundation for treating their reports differently.
McLatchie's proposal to treat apostolic claims as evidence and assess extraordinary reports through the witnesses' credibility and the particulars of each case.
Dillahunty links the failed comparison with other religions to the alien hypothetical and argues that McLatchie's conclusion merely restates confidence in favored witnesses.
Extraordinary reports should be evaluated through witness reliability, incentives to lie, possibilities of honest mistake, and relevant prior probabilities rather than rejected by category alone.
The move supplies the requested criteria for discriminating testimony and incorporates prior probability into the affirmative's comparative explanatory framework.
Dillahunty's charge that McLatchie has no foundation for trusting apostolic resurrection testimony while distrusting analogous alien-abduction testimony.
McLatchie proposes a structured inquiry into witness character, deception, mistake, dreams, and background plausibility, applying the last factor to interstellar visitation.
A natural alien-visitation hypothesis is more antecedently plausible than a violation of known natural regularities, while no resurrection has been independently and scientifically verified.
It invokes background knowledge and the absence of verifiable precedent to argue that first-century literary claims cannot establish a resurrection to a strong evidential standard.
McLatchie's appeal to the allegedly vanishing prior probability of alien visitation and his claim that Jesus is a verifiable resurrection case.
Dillahunty contrasts a physically possible natural event with resurrection, requests a medically verifiable precedent, and denies that a handful of ancient books provides scientific verification.
Evidence for Jesus' resurrection is stronger than the report about Lazarus because it draws on multiple source streams and claimed apostolic witnesses rather than a single Johannine report.
It offers a comparative evidential distinction within Christian miracle claims and identifies multiple attestation and apostolic provenance as reasons to privilege the Jesus case.
Dillahunty's challenge asking why Jesus' resurrection is treated as directly verifiable while Lazarus' resurrection receives only indirect support.

McLatchie grounds the Lazarus report in John's general trustworthiness but argues that Jesus has broader attestation through Paul, Acts, the Gospels, apostolic claimants, and the empty-tomb tradition.
A cumulative case from source trustworthiness, apostolic provenance, and elimination of sincere-error and deception hypotheses makes resurrection the best explanation of the reported encounters.
This is the affirmative's culminating inference for the motion, connecting source credibility and apostolic testimony to comparative elimination of natural testimonial explanations.
Dillahunty's recurring objections that biblical claims are not sufficient evidence, that witness credibility has not been established, and that mistake or fabrication remain preferable explanations.

McLatchie summarizes the inductive reliability case for the Gospels, Acts, and Paul, traces the claim to original apostles, and argues that multisensory encounters and martyrdom weigh against mistake and deceit.

The resurrection is the best explanation after alternatives involving honest mistake or deliberate deception are disconfirmed, and testimonial claims can themselves constitute evidence requiring explanation.
This passage states the pro side's ultimate inference and directly defends the evidential status of the surviving reports at the center of the motion.
Dillahunty's position that the Christian reports are claims rather than adequate evidence for a resurrection.
McLatchie concludes that rival explanations have been weakened and argues that testimonial claims may be evidence whose best explanation is that the reported resurrection occurred.
Witness credibility may support trust in testimony, but the claim itself is not its own evidence, and McLatchie's best-explanation reasoning is abductive rather than inductive.
The passage directly contests both the logical classification and the evidential foundation of the pro side's cumulative best-explanation case.
McLatchie's closing contention that Dillahunty dismisses induction and wrongly separates testimonial claims from evidence.

Dillahunty distinguishes credibility evidence from the proposition asserted, labels the resurrection inference abductive, and rejects the idea that merely asserting a claim supplies evidence for itself.
The apostles' demonstrated habitual truthfulness across the Gospels, Acts, and Pauline material supplies additional evidence that they were not lying about the resurrection.
This supplies an independent route beyond martyrdom for rejecting deliberate deception, one of the principal rival explanations in the pro case.
The question's challenge that martyrdom may be the only meaningful basis for concluding that the apostles were not lying.
Asked for evidence against apostolic deceit beyond martyrdom, McLatchie points to what he regards as broad indications of the authors' habitual historical truthfulness.

Sufficient resurrection evidence can overcome a very low prior probability, while perceived convergences between Jesus' history, scriptural expectations, and Christianity's expansion make the resurrection less antecedently improbable.
The passage answers the central prior-probability objection to miracles and offers affirmative considerations intended to raise the resurrection hypothesis's prior plausibility.
The Humean objection that a miracle is necessarily the least probable explanation and therefore cannot be inferred historically.
McLatchie argues that strong likelihood evidence can outweigh a small prior and invokes Passover symbolism and Christianity's global spread as convergences with earlier messianic expectations.
Lying is more probable than an accurate miracle report, and Dillahunty applies the same skeptical standard to supernatural claims in any historical source rather than singling out the Bible.
This states the con side's comparative-probability objection and rebuts the charge that its historical standard is selectively hostile to Christian sources.
McLatchie's contention that apostolic lying is disfavored and the audience's suggestion that Dillahunty applies a special standard to the Bible.
Dillahunty does not allege actual deception but maintains it would remain likelier than accurate miracle testimony and says he rejects comparable supernatural reports in other historical books too.

If the evidential standard used for biblical resurrection reports would also compel acceptance of analogous religious claims, that parity would undermine the standard and expose an unresolved inconsistency.
The passage tests the selectivity and reliability of the pro side's epistemic method by applying it across competing miracle traditions.
McLatchie's claim that the biblical reports provide reliably strong evidence for resurrection while other religious miracle accounts may be rejected.
Dillahunty asks whether McLatchie's evidential foundation generalizes to rival religions, obtains agreement that such parity would be damaging, and presses for a principled differentiator.

Competing religious reports should be assessed by their case-specific historical particulars; for example, the Quran's late denial of Jesus' crucifixion conflicts with substantially earlier first-century evidence.
This provides the pro side's proposed nonselective criterion for distinguishing Christian historical claims from contrary claims in another religious tradition.
Dillahunty's challenge that McLatchie accepts Christian accounts while dismissing other religions' accounts without a differentiating evidential standard.
McLatchie answers that traditions turn on their individual evidence and uses the Quran's much later denial of crucifixion as an example of a claim defeated by earlier sources.

A report may be a data point without being sufficient evidence for its own proposition; credibility, background knowledge, and consistency with established facts can support ordinary testimony, but multiplying extraordinary claims does not establish a resurrection.
This is the con side's fullest account of why ordinary testimony may be accepted while indirect resurrection reports remain insufficiently supported and untestable.
McLatchie's accusation that Dillahunty falsely separates claims from evidence, together with questions comparing resurrection reports to reports of rape or racism.

Dillahunty distinguishes propositions from supporting considerations, explains how background evidence makes mundane reports credible, and argues that the alleged empty tomb remains only an unverified claim.

Dillahunty's skepticism does not reject miracles as explanations in principle; he would accept that a resurrection occurred if sufficient evidence established the event, while treating its cause as a separate question.
The clarification defines the con position as an evidential objection rather than an a priori naturalistic exclusion of resurrection, directly sharpening the motion-level dispute.
McLatchie's characterization of Dillahunty as holding that miracles are always least probable and can never be the best historical explanation.
Dillahunty says the debate concerns whether the event is adequately evidenced, denies rejecting miracles out of hand, and separates evidence that an event occurred from evidence explaining how.

Literary dependence among the Gospels does not defeat undesigned-coincidence arguments when their interlockings are casual and subtle, as illustrated by details explaining why Jesus addresses Philip before the feeding of the five thousand.
This defends a specific source-reliability argument against the objection that apparent interlockings merely result from Gospel authors copying one another.
The audience challenge that non-deliberate coincidences are improbable or unprovable because the Gospel authors copied from one another.
McLatchie concedes literary dependence but argues that incidental cross-account details about Philip and Bethsaida fit too subtly to look deliberately manufactured and therefore support historicity.
Appealing to magic or a supernatural mystery has no explanatory power because unknowns must be explained through things already understood.
This states the skeptical standard governing whether a supernatural resurrection can function as an explanation rather than merely relabeling the unknown.
The contrary suggestion that rejecting supernatural explanations is an arbitrary non-magic assumption and that magic explains the evidence equally well.
During audience questions, Matt rejects the proposed symmetry between naturalism and non-magic assumptions by arguing that explanation requires intelligible mechanisms.
Resurrection reports must be assessed by source credibility, proximity, habitual reliability, and eyewitness connection, criteria he says favor Jesus over Dionysus.
The move directly defends why the Christian resurrection reports allegedly provide stronger historical evidence than superficially similar ancient religious claims.
The contrary comparison that written religious reports of Dionysus rising should be accepted on the same basis as New Testament resurrection reports.
Jonathan answers an audience challenge about inconsistent treatment of pagan resurrection traditions by offering source-quality criteria rather than accepting every ancient claim equally.
The Jesus case may contain more reports than the Dionysus case, but relative superiority does not establish that the evidence is sufficient to justify resurrection belief.
This directly applies the debate's evidential threshold, arguing that being better supported than a weaker rival does not make an extraordinary conclusion justified.
Jonathan's contrary position that the historically credible, proximate, eyewitness-linked character of Christian sources distinguishes Jesus from Dionysus.
Matt grants a limited comparative advantage to the Jesus tradition while denying that more potential reports amount to enough evidence for accepting a resurrection.
One need not specify in advance every fact that would persuade; compelling evidence requires a demonstrable causal connection to the claim and standards that do not license competing miracles.
The response articulates Matt's governing evidential standard and challenges the resurrection case to avoid lowering that standard enough to admit rival supernatural claims.
The contrary challenge that skepticism is defective unless Matt can specify necessary and sufficient historical evidence that would compel resurrection belief.
Asked what historical evidence would convince him, Matt says unprecedented claims cannot always have advance criteria, but evidence must connect causally and preserve consistent standards.
Multiple positive lines of evidence cumulatively reduce the probability of myth, conspiracy, and hallucination alternatives, thereby increasing support for resurrection.
This is a compact statement of the pro side's cumulative inference: evidence is offered to weaken naturalistic alternatives and redistribute probability toward resurrection.
The contrary challenge that Paul cannot reliably be distinguished from Joseph Smith as truthful rather than dishonest or sincerely mistaken.
Jonathan responds to a comparison between religious claimants by summarizing his cumulative method for discriminating among truth, deception, mistake, and alternative explanations.
Gospel reliability is not inferred from the authors' self-claims but from accuracy on cross-checkable matters, which provides reason for defeasible trust on uncheckable matters.
The move defends the bridge from independently checkable historical details to presumptive trust in gospel claims that cannot themselves be directly corroborated.
The contrary suggestion that an apologetic text merely declares its own witnesses trustworthy and therefore offers a circular basis for accepting them.
Jonathan rejects a circular self-attestation argument and instead presents successful external cross-checking as the basis for extending qualified trust to other gospel content.
Narrative imperfections do not establish historicity because storytellers naturally use exaggeration, hyperbole, and flaws to make accounts more compelling and less suspiciously perfect.
This supplies a rival explanation for apparent narrative roughness, undermining attempts to treat incidental flaws or imperfect symmetry as authenticity indicators.
The contrary reliability inference that realistic, incidental, or imperfect features of gospel narratives count as signs of truthful historical reporting.
Matt uses a magic-performance analogy and ordinary storytelling behavior to argue that flaws can be deliberately or naturally incorporated without making a story historical.
Undesigned coincidences, external corroboration, allusive similarities, and related categories cumulatively support general gospel reliability and defeasible trust in particular assertions.
The passage consolidates the evidential foundation on which the pro case treats the gospel accounts as substantially trustworthy sources for resurrection claims.
The contrary challenge asking how Jonathan knows that the claims used to characterize biblical figures and witnesses as trustworthy are themselves true.
Jonathan answers a question about warrant for biblical trustworthiness by listing mutually reinforcing historical tests and describing the defeasible inference they support.
Despite repeated references to extra-biblical evidence and support, the actual resurrection case presented did not contain anything genuinely extra-biblical.
The objection attacks the claimed independence of corroboration, which is crucial to whether the gospel reliability case escapes reliance on Christian textual assertions alone.
Jonathan's contrary claim that extra-biblical corroborations form one of several independent categories cumulatively supporting gospel reliability.
Immediately after Jonathan lists corroborative categories, Matt argues that the debate presentation repeatedly invoked external support without actually supplying an external component.
A proposition is not itself evidence; contextual facts about the claimant, setting, and circumstances may instead constitute evidence for or against that proposition.
The distinction directly governs whether testimonial resurrection assertions count as evidence themselves or require independently supported contextual facts to acquire evidential force.
The contrary position that claims can themselves be weak evidence, with their evidential status and weight varying according to context.
Matt clarifies the recurring dispute over testimony by separating the asserted proposition from surrounding facts about who asserted it and under what conditions.
